title: Simulating alternate voting systems
beats: Why are two-party systems everywhere if everyone hates them? The voting system.
Three systems to simulate: plurality, instant runoff, approval; each has a flaw and a strategy to fill in.
Multi-winner systems are better but out of scope here.
Model voters on a 1D line, then 2D issue space (apples vs mangoes, modern vs spooky homes), 100 gray voters.
Plurality with two candidates: orange beats green, nothing seems wrong.
Add purple; predict; green wins. Spoiler effect named afterwards.
Purple voters face honesty vs strategy; zero-sum two-party consequence.
Instant runoff stepped through on the same voters; totals match honest then strategic plurality.
IRV lets you vote honestly, then fall back to strategy automatically.
Pause and find the situation where IRV breaks; arrange candidates; center squeeze.
Australia's century of IRV: better but still two dominant parties.
Approval voting with an approval radius drawn as circles.
Same orange/green then add purple: no spoiler, totals unchanged.
Pause: what would you do as a voter? Layer 1: approving all equals not voting.
Layer 2: orange and purple voters betray each other; green creeps up; chicken dilemma, link to hawk-dove video.
Extreme strategy collapses to plurality, but nobody ever drops their true favorite; score voting generalization; no real-world examples.
Plurality is worst; leans approval; vote every time.

new_moves.name: each-fix-has-a-flaw-template
new_moves.what: Announce up front that every system will have a flaw plus a strategy to fill in, then complete the same table for each

new_moves.name: learner-finds-the-counterexample
new_moves.what: Ask the viewer to arrange candidates to break the system before showing the arrangement

new_moves.name: strategy-as-layers
new_moves.what: Peel strategic behaviour in layers, each simulated as a rule voters follow

theory: The video fixes one tiny scene (orange, green, then purple) and reruns it under each rule, so the learner compares systems by watching the same stimulus produce different outcomes. Each system's flaw is found by the viewer by trying to break it, not by being told. The teaching unit is the counterexample.
velocity: Scene builder: provide a reusable fixed scenario that can be re-run under different rules for side-by-side comparison.
Orchestrator: for any 'design' topic, add a find-the-flaw pause where the learner places elements to break the rule.
Voice: name phenomena (spoiler, center squeeze) after the behaviour is seen.
Learner model: track which flaw the learner found before reveal.
Evals: check the final verdict is committed with stated tradeoffs.
quote: Do they vote for their honest favorite, or strategically vote for second choice
